newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia faces AIDS epidemic, launches safe sex ads.
newsitem.headline: Russia faces AIDS epidemic, launches safe sex ads.

text.p: Russia is facing an AIDS epidemic as the number of people carrying the HIV virus has rocketed in the past year, officials and international medical workers said on Thursday at the launch of a new public awareness campaign.
"The outlook is extremely pessimistic," Alexander Goliusov, chief specialist at the Health Ministry's AIDS prevention department, told a news conference.

Up to 800,000 of Russia's 150 million people could be infected by the year 2000 compared with just a few thousand now, according to a health expert quoted by Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders), the international charity which launched the safe sex campaign with the ministry.

In the first five months of 1997 alone, the number of people officially infected with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, increased by nearly 80 percent. Last year, the number of new registered cases was more than the total for the previous nine years, since the first case was diagnosed in the Soviet Union.
The number of recorded cases is still small -- 4,494 people at the end of May, 259 of them with AIDS itself. But Goliusov said the real figure was probably two or three times that.
And he warned that the days when Russians, once protected by Soviet social controls, could regard AIDS as a foreigners' plague were coming to an end.
"The current situation is very sharply different," Goliusov said. "Russia has entered a new phase of the epidemic."

Although at present 76 percent of HIV sufferers in Russia are intravenous drug users, the potential for rapid growth through sexual contact is underlined by an astonishing 60-fold increase in syphilis infection over the past eight years.

In 1988, syphilis was about as rare in the Soviet Union as in western Europe. Now, nearly 400,000 Russians are infected, an epidemic experts warn is more due to a relaxation of compulsory health controls and to economic upheaval that to the widely perceived post-communist sexual revolution.

The latest anti-AIDS campaign, which follows earlier awareness programmes in the early 1990s, is aimed at 15- to 24-year-olds in Moscow. Officials hope it will serve as a pilot for other cities which are even more badly affected.

The "Safe Sex, My Choice" slogan will be carried on television and radio, buses and billboards and in the press in an effort to convince young people, already well aware of the disease, to use condoms to protect themselves.

Medecins sans Frontieres is also promoting separate targetted programmes to educate young drug users in the dangers of AIDS and schemes to provide information and training for Russian medical workers.
